steps.title: Past twenty, the rules change again
body: You already know 1-10, and that 3-10 take a plural noun in an unusual reversed-gender form (see the counting rule from earlier). From eleven on, the whole system shifts once more: the counted noun goes back to singular — but now in the accusative case, not the noun's usual form.

أَحَدَ عَشَرَ (11) and اثْنَا عَشَرَ (12) are irregular compounds, best learned as their own pair. From 13 to 19 there's a real system: the ones-digit keeps the reversed agreement you already know from 3-10, while the "-teen" part (عَشَر/عَشْرَة) agrees normally with the noun instead — the two halves point in opposite directions on purpose.

20 through 90 stop caring about gender entirely — عِشْرُونَ counts anything. Compounds like 21 just glue a ones-digit onto a tens word with وَ. And مِائَة (100) breaks pattern a third time: it takes a genitive noun, the same government 3-10 use, not the accusative 11-99 use.

steps.title: Eleven to a hundred
steps.intro: Read each number, then the seven example sentences. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: Singular, not plural
steps.prompt: Why is كِتَابًا singular here, not a plural like كُتُب?

options.label: 11-99 take a singular accusative noun, unlike 3-10's plural
"Book" has no plural form in Arabic
It's a mistake — plurals are always used after a number

steps.explanation: From 11 up, the counted noun switches to singular accusative (تمييز) — كِتَابًا, not the plural genitive كُتُبٍ that 3-10 use.

steps.title: Does twenty change?
steps.prompt: Does عِشْرُونَ change when counting a feminine noun?

options.label: No — 20 through 90 are invariant for gender
Yes, it takes a feminine ending
Yes, it becomes a completely different word

steps.explanation: عِشْرُونَ counts طَالِبَة and كِتَاب alike — the tens words stopped caring about gender entirely, the first number words in the course to do so.

steps.title: Hundred breaks the pattern again
steps.prompt: What case is كِتَابٍ in, and why?

options.label: Genitive — مِائَة governs a genitive noun through iḍāfa, the same government 3-10 use
Accusative — every number from 11 up uses accusative
Nominative — كِتَابٍ is the subject of the sentence

steps.explanation: مِائَة doesn't follow 11-99's own rule — it takes a singular genitive noun via iḍāfa (مِائَةُ كِتَابٍ), a third pattern alongside 3-10's plural genitive and 11-99's singular accusative.

steps.title: You can count to a hundred
steps.message: You've now met all three of Arabic's counting patterns: 1-2 use the noun's own form, 3-10 take a reversed-gender plural, and 11-99 take a singular accusative noun instead — with 11, 12, and مِائَة each bending the rule in their own way. Telling time, dates, and prices build on this later.
